summary: Describes an RTP payload format for comfort noise, the soft background hiss played during silence. It is for audio codecs, like G.711, that cannot carry comfort noise themselves.

plainLanguage.summary: A completely silent phone line feels like the call dropped. This tells how to send a quiet fake hum during pauses so the line sounds alive.

questions: how is comfort noise sent over rtp
what is a silence insertion descriptor
subtitle: A tiny RTP payload that tells the listener how loud and what color the background hiss should be during silence.

tldr.problem: Audio codecs such as G.711 have no built-in way to describe background noise, so silence suppression can leave the listener with dead air.
tldr.mechanism: A comfort noise payload carries one byte for the noise level and optionally one byte per reflection coefficient that shapes the noise, sent in the same RTP stream with its own payload type.
tldr.outcome: The format is a minimum interoperability specification; how noise is analysed, generated and when packets are sent stays up to the implementation.

today: RFC 3389 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Comfort Noise
sections.content:
RFC 3389 defines an RTP payload format for comfort noise (CN). It is meant mainly for audio codecs with no discontinuous transmission (DTX) of their own, such as ITU-T G.711, G.726, G.727, G.728 and G.722. It is based on Appendix II of ITU-T G.711.

The payload is also called a Silence Insertion Descriptor (SID) frame. The RFC specifies only the payload. Comfort noise analysis and synthesis, voice activity detection (VAD) and DTX algorithms are left to implementations. An earlier version that carried only the noise level byte was in drafts of RFC 1890, and the extended format should be backward compatible if implementations read only the first byte.
sections.plainLanguage: When people stop talking, the sender sends a short note about the background hum instead of the hum itself, and the listener's phone makes a similar hum.

sections.title: VAD, DTX and Noise Generation
sections.content:
The RFC describes the usual parts of a codec with DTX. Voice activity detection (VAD) separates active from inactive speech. During inactive segments a comfort noise generator (CNG) describes the ambient noise while keeping the transmission rate low. The DTX algorithm decides when a CN payload is sent. During active speech, packets of the voice codec go out, marked by that codec's payload type.

At the receiver, the CNG uses each CN payload to update its noise model and produces a suitable amount of comfort noise. The RFC says an example solution for G.711 was tested and is described in Appendix II of ITU-T G.711, using the VAD and DTX of G.729 Annex B.
sections.plainLanguage: One part notices when nobody is talking, another decides when to send the hum note, and the listener's side turns the note into a quiet hum.

sections.title: The CN Payload
sections.content:
The first byte is the noise level. The top bit is unused and always 0, and the lower 7 bits give the level in -dBov, where values 0 to 127 stand for 0 to -127 dBov. dBov is a level relative to the overload point of the system.

Optional spectral information follows as reflection coefficients of an all-pole model of the noise. Each coefficient lies between -1 and 1 and is quantized uniformly to an 8-bit index N from 0 to 254; index 255 is reserved for future use. The model order M is not sent, because the receiver derives it from the payload length. The total payload is M+1 bytes, and a model of order 0 is just the noise level. A decoder may ignore higher-order coefficients by treating them as zero.
sections.plainLanguage: The first byte says how loud the hum is. Any extra bytes describe its flavor, such as how deep or hissy it sounds.

sections.title: Using CN in RTP and SDP
sections.content:
The RTP header for a CN packet SHOULD be built as if comfort noise were an independent codec, and the RTP timestamp marks the start of the comfort noise period. Under the RTP profile of RFC 1890, static payload type 13 is assigned for a timestamp clock rate of 8,000 Hz; other rates MUST use dynamic payload types. The marker bit SHOULD NOT be set. Each CN packet MUST contain exactly one CN payload per channel, and with several channels all use the same model order.

A CN packet is sent at the start of a silence period in the same RTP stream as the speech. How often it is updated is left to the implementation: periodically, or only when the background noise changes noticeably.

In SDP, CN is announced by listing its payload type, for example m=audio 49230 RTP/AVP 0 13 for G.711 with CN. For other clock rates an rtpmap attribute such as CN/16000 is needed. If CN is not listed, the format is not used, but silence may still be suppressed. A receiver can notice this when the timestamp jumps although the sequence number advanced by one.
sections.plainLanguage: The hum note travels in the same stream as the voice, with its own label so the receiver knows what it is, and the call setup lists that label if both sides agree to use it.

sections.title: IANA and Security
sections.content:
The RFC registers the RTP payload name and MIME type audio/CN, with an optional rate parameter that defaults to 8000 and should match the codec used alongside it. It also assigns payload type 13.

Security follows the RTP specification, so confidentiality comes from encrypting the media stream, and encryption MAY be applied after encapsulation. Because the format only transports background noise, the RFC says there are no significant security, confidentiality or authentication concerns.
sections.plainLanguage: The format has an official name and number in the registry. Since it only carries a quiet hum, there is not much worth stealing.
